exam: A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with painful defecation and occasional blood – what investigations would you prioritize and why? — DRE, stool microscopy, and ultrasound to rule out opportunistic infection, parasite, and obstructive lesion.

A child in a rural clinic has hard stools and abdominal discomfort – which management steps are appropriate first? — Give osmotic laxative, advise increased fluid/fibre, and perform DRE to confirm impaction.
How does dyschezia differ from dysphagia in history taking? — Dyschezia focuses on bowel habits, pain on stool passage; dysphagia on swallowing difficulty and throat pain.

A patient on long‑term morphine develops dyschezia – what medication change would you consider? — Switch to a non‑opioid analgesic or add a peripherally acting opioid antagonist (e.g., methylnaltrexone) to restore motility.
What red‑flag signs would prompt urgent surgical referral? — Signs of obstruction (no flatus), peritonitis, massive rectal bleeding, or perforation.

Explain why a normal abdominal X‑ray does not exclude colonic stricture in a patient with chronic dyschezia. — Early strictures may not cause visible dilatation; ultrasound or CT is needed if symptoms persist.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a patient with dyschezia also has fever and diarrhoea – which infection is most likely and how treat? — Consider amoebic dysentery; treat with metronidazole followed by a luminal agent.
What is the role of the Bristol Stool Chart in assessing dyschezia? — Categorises stool form to differentiate constipation (type 1‑2) from diarrhoea (type 6‑7) and guides therapy.
ai.title: Dyschezia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Dyschezia is painful or difficult defecation caused by functional, structural or systemic factors. In low‑resource settings, common causes include constipation, obstructive lesions, infections and medication side‑effects.

sections.p: Dyschezia describes pain or effortful passage of stool. It reflects a problem anywhere from the rectum to the colon and can be functional or organic.
Identify the underlying mechanism: motility disorder, obstruction, inflammation or systemic disease. Classify severity with the Bristol Stool Chart and pain score.

sections.p: Unrelieved dyschezia can lead to fecal impaction, megacolon, electrolyte loss and sepsis. In low‑resource hospitals, delayed presentation is common.
